results.title: The Silver Brumby: Bravery in the Bush
results.brief_description: From the classic Australian feature film, videos and TV series based on the much loved novels by Elyne Mitchell comes this new CD ROM. Untamed by man and unbroken in spirit, the Silver Brumby captures all the drama and spirit of Australian animals in their natural habitat, while teaching children about the importance of protecting our wildlife and assisting reading and comprehension skills. This CD ROM features 20 beautifully illustrated storybook pages, with several alternate conclusions, as well as 8 fun and challenging puzzles to solve. Suitable for ages 3-8.

results.title: The Exorcist
results.creator_credit: William Friedkin, William Peter Blatty and Warner Bros Pictures
results.brief_description: The Exorcist occupies a central position in the history of horror films, an almost sadistically malevolent experience in terror. Regan (Linda Blair) is a young girl entering puberty and she becomes possessed by the spirit of an ancient demon. Her mother (Ellen Burstyn) finds that there is no assistance in the scientific pragmatism of the modern world and she hesitantly turns to the occult rites of Catholicism and Orthodoxy in order to rid her daughter of the monster. The exorcism scenes attain a disturbing authenticity and they are based on the official Catholic Church rites of exorcism. “The Exorcist” is a film that feeds on our most intimate fears and terrors and not a film for the easily frightened. Stars Max Van Sydow as Father Merrin. Based on the book by William Peter Blatty. Mercedes McCambridge is the voice of the Devil. Part of Tubular Bell by Mike Oldfield used on the soundtrack.

constellations_other.name: Haunted spaces
constellations_other.description: Films about demonic possession use architecture and environment to heighten fear. Late Night with the Devil places evil in a 1970s TV studio, connecting works where sets, buildings and media spaces shape horror, tension and supernatural menace.

results.title: Tank girl
results.creator_credit: Rachel Talalay, John Watson, Pen Densham, Richard Lewis, Trilogy Entertainment Group and United Artists Corporation
results.brief_description: The year is 2033 and water is a precious commodity. In the desolate wind swept plains, animals are banned, bathing is unheard of, and the Water & Power Company, headed by the villainous Kesslee (Malcolm McDowell), have ultimate control over the precious H20. One rebel girl stands in their way, Rebecca (Lori Petty), a chick with attitude and an outrageous hairstyle. She is captured by Water & Power when they kill her boyfriend, kidnap her young friend, and try to blackmail her into joining their team. As a prisoner Rebecca discovers a new passion- tanks, and makes a friend with mechanic and pilot, Jet Girl (Naomi Watts), who helps her escape. Once free the girls join forces with The Rippers, an army of half men and half kangaroos, genetically modified to be the ultimate fighting machines. Together they take Water & Power head on, lead by Jet Girl in the sky, and tank girl on the ground with her beloved tank in a flurry of live action and comic strip visuals. Cast also includes Ice-T, Don Harvey and Jeff Kober.

constellations_primary.name: Dystopian futures & horrific pasts
constellations_primary.description: For an industry that leans strongly toward happy endings, it's interesting to note that a lot of futures that are speculated in film are dystopic.  However we don't need to look too far to find horrors in the past and present.

results.title: The Red balloon = Le Ballon rouge
results.brief_description: A small boy finds a balloon which follows him everywhere and fills his need for friendship. When the balloon ultimately lifts the child to the sky, it’s a liberating expression of the freedom of childhood. Based on the story by Albert Lamorisse. No dialogue. (Awards: Academy Award, Best Original Screenplay; Cannes, Best Short Film)

constellations_other.name: Outliers of the Hollywood musical
constellations_other.description: It might feel like the musical genre has been resting since the golden age of cinema, but you only need to look at how many music videos have been produced - especially since the launch of MTV in 1981 - to realise that it isn't. These days, if we count narrative-based music videos, the overwhelming majority that are made are short, snappy and live outside of the Hollywood studio system.

results.title: Dancer in the dark
results.creator_credit: Lars Von Trier, Vibeke Windelov, Arte France, France 3 Cinema, Trust Film Svenska and Zentropa Entertainment
results.brief_description: ‘Dancer in the dark’ is simultaneously an ode to the Hollywood musical, an experiment in digital filmmaking, and a wholly unique, landmark film in contemporary cinema. Similar to ‘Breaking the waves’ and ‘The Idiots’, it centres on a martyr-like female character who is put through excruciating sacrifice and suffering. The setting is rural, 1950s America. Selma (played by Icelandic pop star, Bjork), a Czech immigrant, works day and night to save money for an eye operation that will prevent her son from inheriting an eyesight condition that currently plagues her. What Selma lacks in vision, she makes up for in imagination. ‘Dancer in the dark’ is punctuated with extended fantasy musical sequences in which the drabness of the everyday is transformed into something fantastic, joyous, rhythmic and utopian. Though she enjoys the support of friends, including her best friend Kathy (Catherine Deneuve) and neighbour Bill (David Morse), and is active in the local theatre group, things go from bad to worse for Selma. Loss of financial security and crude betrayal leads to murder, death and an overall Herculean sense of tragedy. Von Trier does many fascinating things in this film. Though he partakes in the Dogme tradition - which seeks to strip away the complete artifice of cinema and usher in the ‘real’ through only ‘natural’ means - Von Trier also reworks and questions it. He does so by juxtaposing documentary-style, almost ‘home-video’ footage, with extremely dazzling, technologically sophisticated, emotionally delirious musical numbers. By throwing together opposite cinematic styles, pushing the characters, the story and the audience to absolute limits of emotional intensity and melodrama, Von Trier not only brings out the essence of the musical as a boundless, overwhelming force, but also asks questions about cinema itself and its powers of storytelling in a post-modern, digital age.

results.title: The Man Who Fell to Earth
results.creator_credit: Nicolas Roeg, Barry Spikings, Michael Deeley and British Lion Films
results.brief_description: David Bowie, plays The Stranger. Armed with a British passport, he arrives in New York but is in fact an alien from a dying planet, having studied earth habits from monitoring television. This hairless, sexless creature is eventually caught and handed over to a team of scientists and doctors for research. Nicolas Roeg’s technical brilliance is apparent in this weirdly voyeuristic science fiction fantasy which is at times emeshed in its convoluted plot. Co-starring Buck Henry as a patent lawyer who befriends The Stranger and reaps success from the acquaintance and Rip Torn as Professor Nathan Brycce, determined to discover the truth.
results.creator_credit_for_label: Nicolas Roeg, Barry Spikings, Michael Deeley and British Lion Films
results.description:
“David Bowie’s journey from a heartbroken alien trapped on earth to a powerful and wealthy entrepreneur is a mad and imaginative ride that is as relevant as ever.” – filmmaker and The Future & Other Fictions advisory group member Robert Connolly.

results.title: Clint Eastwood
results.creator_credit: Ray Atherton and Passport International Entertainment
results.brief_description:
Episode of Series “Hollywood remembers”.
Speak softly and carry a big gun…that’s the attitude that has made Clint Eastwood one of the biggest box office stars! And this video looks at his entire film career, from the early “Spaghetti Westerns”made in Italy to his Hollywood superstar years with “Dirty Harry” and beyond. Featured are rare film clips, original coming attractions, previews, and more, including footage never released to television. It’s a treasure trove featuring Eastwood’s best work, and the first serious retrospective of his lengthy acting career. Whether you’re an Eastwood fan, a film buff, or an action-adventure afficionado, this is a video you’ll want to watch over and over again.

results.title: Rotted Luck
results.brief_description:
Rotted Luck envisions a slot machine overtaken by a living fungal network, playfully critiquing the addictive potential of gaming and gambling. The spinning reel displays familiar slot machine icons like cherries and lemons, but this game unfolds differently. The fruit spins uncontrollably and starts to decay as mould spreads across the screen. As you play, your movements are tracked through a cloud of spores that ultimately engulfs you.

Rotted Luck disrupts the usual interactivity and visual style of slot machines to encourage a stranger, shared and more joyful experience. By subverting conventional game mechanics, it proposes an outcome that isn’t about ‘winning’. Communal, non-addictive and movement-based, Rotted Luck favours the fun of play.

To create the piece, artists Vidya Rajan and Ian MacLarty studied slot machine design and imagined a fungus mistaking one for food. They photographed real decaying fruit, transformed them into 3D models, and used a common webcam to track player movements.

results.title: Anti-Cancer Council ad: Warren Mitchell
results.brief_description: This television advertisement made by the Anti-Cancer Council of Victoria (now Cancer Council Victoria) formed part of the first Australian anti-tobacco advertising campaign which launched on 5 June 1971. Taking a stark and satirical tone, this campaign aimed to undermine the glamourisation of smoking created by cigarette company advertising.
